contributions.statement: When an agent ports or rewrites a module and also ports its tests, do not accept the agent's own ported suite as the equivalence oracle; run the original tests unchanged or a suite produced independently, because test porters silently drop tests for features the port lost (one agent's output passed 93.5% of its own ported suite but 66.2% of an independently ported one).
contributions.evidence: §5.3 reports, as a qualitative observation with no counts, that each system's TestTranslator skipped tests for features its own translation failed to preserve. Table 2: Claude Code's output passes its own suite more often than RustPrint's suite in 8 of 8 repos (mean 93.5% vs 66.2%). Caveats: single run, suite sizes unreported, the cross-suite tests were adapted by a GPT-5.4 agent so some failures may be adaptation errors, and Claude Code's model and setup are unstated.

contributions.statement: After an agent rewrites a module, regenerate a feature-level description from the new code and diff it against the description of the old code to produce a list of possibly dropped features for human review or test writing; do not treat the diff score as proof of equivalence.
contributions.evidence: §3.2 and Fig. 3: the documentation comparison drives repairs, and most of the FCV gain arrives in the first one or two iterations. FCV is the same LLM-judged signal being optimized, the judge has no human validation, and the same Claude Code output scores 52.5% or 48.9% depending on the judge (Fig. 2), so the measured gain is circular.

reason: The objective results (compilation and safe rates) are by-construction stopping criteria of the pipeline, and its documentation-first idea is never ablated, so nothing about pre-translation documentation transfers as evidence. What survives is a weakly evidenced refinement of known 'do not trust self-generated oracles' practice (test porters drop tests for lost features) and a doc-diff gap checklist; both are hypotheses.
